Thanks Rachel — quick operational counter-proposal below (happy to iterate).

Suggested positions for customer-facing counter:
- Uptime: 99.9% for Hosted API (shared pool); 99.95% for Dedicated instances / isolated capacity. Rationale: shared multi-tenant workloads have more variance; dedicated pools have stricter guarantees.
- Credits: replace their table with a tiered pro-rata model: credit = (minutes of downtime / total monthly minutes) * monthly fee for the affected service, subject to a monthly cap of 30% of fees for that service. No per-incident minimum credit.
- Response times: commit to P1 initial response within 30 minutes (24/7), P2 within 4 hours (business hours) with an escalation path to on-call engineering. We can include an optional add-on SLA for 15-min P1 response for enterprise Dedicated customers.
- Maintenance windows: allow rolling maintenance windows up to 4 hours per week for Hosted; for Dedicated, agree up to 2 hours weekly if scheduled 7 days out. Emergency maintenance allowed for security-critical patches with as much notice as possible and an audit log of the change.
- Exclusions: clearly call out DDOS beyond mitigation control, force majeure, customer-caused incidents, and scheduled maintenance as exclusions to uptime calculations.

If legal signs off on drafting that back as a redline, we should also include an implementation note in the Order Form listing which hosts/regions are covered by the SLA.

—Marissa
Sr. Manager, Technical Account Management

Legal notes / redline guidance — drafting points I want in the counter redline:

- Keep uptime language measurable: specify measurement methodology (rolling 30-day window, exclude scheduled maintenance windows, define metric endpoints and ingress hosts).
- For credits, avoid absolute tables tied to minutes; the pro-rata monthly model Marissa suggested is cleaner and easier to implement. Define the cap (30%) and an annual cap on cumulative credits if needed.
- Response SLA: we can accept a 30-min P1 initial response as standard and offer 15-min for Dedicated at higher commitment/price. Avoid committing to fix times (MTTR) — use acknowledgment and escalation steps.
- Maintenance notice: include a clause that "Redwood will provide reasonable advance notice of scheduled maintenance (typically >=7 days) except for security or emergency remediation, in which case Redwood will provide notice as soon as practicable." This gives us flexibility.
- Audit & evidence: we can provide availability reports and incident summaries on request (once per quarter) and on-demand for escalations — but avoid continuous real-time transparency obligations.

If you want, I can bake these into the doc and produce Redwood_counter_sla_redline.pdf for your review.

—Kimberly
Senior Counsel, Contracts & Security
